title: Neural target scaler is fitted on the NOISY labels, so every neural uncertainty is multiplied by a factor that grows with the noise level
what_the_code_does: run_neural_experiment passes `y_noisy` into train_neural_regression as `y_train` (line 1254-1256). train_neural_regression then does `y_scaler = StandardScaler(); y_scaler.fit_transform(y_train)` (867-869) and keeps `y_scale = y_scaler.scale_[0]` (872), i.e. the standard deviation of the CORRUPTED training labels at that noise level. At line 962 the per-molecule uncertainty is converted back to label units as `std_raw = preds_norm.std(0) * y_scale`. Because the injected noise is independent of the label, sd(y_noisy) = sqrt(sd_clean^2 + dose^2), so y_scale rises monotonically with the noise level while sd_clean stays fixed.
other_pipeline: QM9 standardises the target in Rust with the CLEAN training mean and spread — rust/src/main.rs:1798-1800, whose own comment says 'Standardise with the CLEAN training mean and spread. Standardising with the noisy spread (the old behaviour) moved the target scale with the noise level'. The QM9 neural models therefore have no noise-dependent multiplier on their uncertainties.
consequence: Every reported uncertainty from BNN-Full, VBLL-Full, MLP-BNN-Full and MLP-VBLL-Full on LogD/Caco-2/hERG is multiplied by sqrt(1 + (dose/sd_clean)^2) purely because of the scaler, before the model has done anything. The anchored grids are designed to run the dose up to roughly the label spread, so at the top of a grid this is a large mechanical inflation. Any claim of the form 'the Bayesian nets' intervals widen as noise rises', and any coverage-at-1sd/2sd number for those four models, is partly or wholly this factor; and it is not comparable with the QM9 neural rows, which do not carry it. Fix: fit y_scaler on the clean training labels (pass them in) rather than on y_noisy.

title: "SNS" keeps substructure counts on the experimental side and is bit-packed to binary on QM9, destroying the counts QM9 computed
what_the_code_does: create_sns is called with sub_counts defaulting to True, and _transform_sns writes `features[i, idx] = count` — the raw multiplicity of each retained substructure — into a float32 (n, 1024) array. Verified by running it on five molecules: dtype float32, max value 34.0, ~0.9% of nonzero entries greater than 1. Atom invariants are `GetMorganAtomInvGen(includeRingMembership=True)`, useBondTypes=True, includeChirality=False, radius 2; the vocabulary is the top 1024 substructure ids sorted by `(prevalence, sub_id)` descending, so the ranking is fully deterministic with no RNG.
consequence: On QM9 the SNS feature matrix is a binary indicator of the top-1024 substructures; on the validation sets it is a count matrix over the same 1024 slots. Tree models split differently on counts than on indicators, and z-scored counts feed a completely different RBF geometry to SVM/GP. Any claim that SNS ranks the same way on QM9 and on the validation sets, and the paper's framing of SNS as ECFP4's collision-free counterpart (ECFP4 is binary on the experimental side, SNS is counts), rest on a representation that is not the same object in the two pipelines.
other_pipeline: scripts/process_and_train.py:988-1046 builds the identical Sort & Slice featuriser with sub_counts=True — it genuinely computes counts (line 1029: sub_id repeated `count` times, then summed). Then scripts/process_and_train.py:474-476 does `np.array(sns_fp, dtype=np.uint8)` followed by `np.packbits(...)`, and the reader at scripts/process_and_train.py:1269 does `np.unpackbits(...)`. packbits maps any nonzero to 1, so the multiplicity is computed and then thrown away. The uint8 cast also wraps any count that is a multiple of 256 to 0.
